name: White vinegar soaks

lead: A white vinegar soak means immersing hands, feet or the body in water that has distilled white vinegar added. People use it for rough or dry-looking skin, foot odour and itchy, flaky patches, with the goal of skin that looks and feels cleaner and calmer.

Research on the practice is thin. A small study of arm soaks in diluted apple cider vinegar found no difference in skin bacteria compared with plain water, and a Cleveland Clinic dermatologist cites studies showing little effect on skin integrity.

paras: In general terms, people dilute white vinegar in a basin or bath of water and soak the skin for several minutes, then pat dry and moisturise. WebMD and the National Eczema Association describe vinegar baths for itchy skin, and Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Gowri Kabbur says she prefers dilute white vinegar to apple cider vinegar.

White vinegar is an acid (typically 5 to 8 percent acetic acid before dilution), and strong solutions can irritate or burn skin. Health sites advise dilution, patch-testing and checking with a dermatologist first for people with eczema or sensitive skin.

chain: Soak skin in diluted white vinegar
Mild acid contact reduces surface bacteria and softens rough skin (as users describe)
angle.text: People soak hands, feet or the body in diluted white vinegar hoping for smoother, calmer, fresher-smelling skin. Advocates describe it as a low-cost home skin treatment.

lead: A white vinegar soak is a folk skin practice in which hands, feet or the body are soaked in water to which distilled white vinegar has been added. People use it chasing smoother, cleaner-looking skin, less foot odour and calmer flaky or itchy patches [1][2].

White vinegar is a fermented dilution of acetic acid, about 5 to 8 percent, with a pH near 2.6 [1]. Vinegar has a long history in folk medicine, from Babylonian and Greek uses onward [1]. Skin soaks draw on that tradition and on the idea that mild acidity helps with bacteria and skin pH.

Few human studies have tested vinegar soaks. A small study described by MyEczemaTeam had participants soak one arm in diluted apple cider vinegar and the other in water for two weeks and found no difference in skin bacteria [3]. Dermatologists quoted by health outlets say evidence is limited and advise dilution [2][4][3].

paras: A soak combines white vinegar with water in a basin or tub; the skin is submerged for a short period. Foot soaks are used for odour and rough skin, hand soaks for dryness, and whole-body vinegar baths for itchy skin conditions such as eczema [2].
White vinegar is made by fermenting distilled alcohol and diluted to roughly 5 to 8 percent acetic acid [1]. Solutions above 10 percent acetic acid are described as corrosive to skin [1].

Proponents say the acidity can reduce itch-causing bacteria on the skin and soften dead surface skin. WebMD describes a vinegar bath as potentially killing some of the bacteria that contribute to itching [2].
Dr. Kabbur says in the Cleveland Clinic podcast: "I prefer the dilute white vinegar more than the apple cider vinegar." [4]

No controlled trial of white vinegar soaks for cosmetic skin appearance has been located. A small study of 11 people with atopic dermatitis and 11 without, soaking one arm in diluted apple cider vinegar and the other in water for 10 minutes daily over two weeks, found no difference in skin bacteria [3]. Dr. Kabbur cites studies showing little effect of apple cider vinegar on the skin microbiome or skin integrity [4].

Strong acetic acid can damage skin [1]. The National Eczema Association, as reported by MyEczemaTeam, warns that overuse can cause chemical burns and advises stopping if skin burns or changes, and suggests patch testing a small area first [3].
